planting.note: Set out divisions or container plants in spring in humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil in partial shade; this sprawling Himalayan species is the wild parent behind many long-blooming hybrid geraniums sold as named cultivars.

directions: Plant in reliably moist, fertile soil in partial shade or morning sun, where the trailing stems can scramble over neighboring plants or spill down a bank. Wallich's cranesbill produces five-petaled violet-blue flowers with a distinctive pale to white eye from midsummer well into autumn, each bloom held above lobed, softly hairy foliage on wiry, sprawling stems that root readily where they touch soil. Unlike its many named selections and hybrids bred for sterility and nonstop bloom, the straight species sets some seed and self-sows modestly in congenial sites. Cut back hard after the first flush in a hot summer to encourage a fresh round of foliage and bloom into fall.

planting.note: Plant crown divisions in spring or fall in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; this Japanese species is one of the principal wild parents of the popular Astilbe x arendsii garden hybrids.

directions: Grow in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, since this species is less tolerant of dry conditions than most garden astilbe hybrids. Thunberg's astilbe produces airy, gracefully arching sprays of small white to pale pink flowers held well above ferny, compound foliage, a looser and more pendulous effect than the stiffly upright plumes typical of arendsii-type cultivars. It blooms slightly later in the summer than many hybrid astilbes, extending the display in a shaded border or woodland-edge planting. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring to maintain vigorous flowering.
sources: Great Plant Picks (Elisabeth C. Miller Botanical Garden)

planting.note: Start seed indoors in a gritty mix 6-8 weeks before the last frost, or divide established clumps in spring; plant out in lean, sharply drained, alkaline soil in full sun, as for most rock-garden pinks.

directions: Grow in lean, sharply drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun, the same conditions preferred by most mat-forming alpine dianthus. Wood pink forms dense tufts of narrow, blue-green grassy foliage topped in early to midsummer by single, bright pink to rose flowers with a faintly fringed edge, carried singly or a few to a wiry stem well above the mat. It is native to rocky limestone slopes and screes across the mountains of southern and central Europe, and performs best in a rock garden, wall crevice, or raised bed where its roots stay dry and cool. Shear lightly after bloom to keep the foliage mat tidy and encourage a looser rebloom later in summer.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in gritty, well-drained soil in partial shade; this Pacific Northwest native tolerates rocky, lean sites that would stress most other alumroots.

directions: Plant in gritty, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, siting it on a slope or in a rock garden where water moves through quickly, mimicking the talus slopes and rocky canyons of its native Pacific Northwest range. Gooseberryleaf alumroot forms a low rosette of rounded, lobed leaves resembling those of its gooseberry namesake, sending up slender, wiry stems in late spring carrying small, loosely spaced white to pink bell-shaped flowers. It is more drought-tolerant than the shade-loving eastern alumroots once established, making it a good choice for a dry rock garden or lean native border. Avoid heavy, wet soils, which are the most common cause of crown rot in this species.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-10 weeks before the last frost, chilling moist sown trays for two to three weeks to break dormancy; plant out in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade after frost danger passes.

directions: Grow in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, conditions similar to the Himalayan foothill meadows where this species grows wild. Fragrant columbine bears nodding, soft creamy-white to pale lilac flowers with a notably sweet, strong fragrance uncommon among columbines, held above finely divided blue-green foliage from late spring into early summer. It is shorter-lived than many garden columbines and benefits from allowing some seed to set and self-sow nearby to maintain a planting over the years. Site it where its scent can be appreciated up close, such as near a path or seating area, and protect from hot afternoon sun, which shortens bloom life.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-10 weeks before the last frost, chilling moist sown trays for two to three weeks to break dormancy; plant out in gritty, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun after frost danger passes.

directions: Grow in gritty, well-drained soil in partial shade or full sun in cooler climates, a lean site similar to the rocky slopes of northern China and Mongolia where this diminutive species grows wild. Green-flowered columbine produces small, nodding, unusual chocolate-brown-and-green or purple-and-green bicolor flowers with short spurs, held just above finely divided, compact foliage, a subtle color combination that appeals to collectors of unusual columbines. Its small stature and quiet coloring suit a rock garden or trough planting where it can be viewed up close rather than a border display. Like most species columbines it is short-lived but self-sows modestly in congenial gritty soil, maintaining a planting over several seasons.
